objective.failText: Haverick's men get into the hall before the bell is freed. It is stopped, in the end, but not before the bravos have done enough damage to the casting floor that the first wards will take a year to be heard properly again.
objective.successText: The doors hold. The Mother Bell rings with every voice in the land, and the Gloam goes back into the deep places.

after.narrate: When it is over, the casting hall is very quiet, in the ordinary way, and very warm.
Orin is sitting with his back to the iron doors. He did not hold them. Hal did, with her company, who came up the mountain behind Haverick's men without being asked.

Orin is sitting with his back to the iron doors. He did not hold them, at the end. Hal did. She came up the mountain in her guild coat, and when she saw who Haverick's men were fighting, she took it off and turned round.
Orin is sitting with his back to the iron doors. He held them the first time, in the night. The second time, he did not have to.

after.text: Somebody else held the door.
How was it?
Terrible. I'd like to do it again.
I had your back the whole time, you know. You never looked round once.
Didn't need to.

after.narrate: Pell Haverick is found the next morning, at the bottom of the mountain, in a coach with a great deal of money and no driver. The miners hand him to the council. The council, for once, agrees on something immediately.

Elske Marrow sits on the casting floor under the Mother Bell, alone, with ink on two fingers and her hands in her lap. The council's delegates are coming up the mountain road. Somebody will have to decide what to do with her. Before that, somebody has to decide what the Mother Bell is for.

Elske Marrow sits on the casting floor under the Mother Bell, alone, with ink on two fingers and her hands in her lap. The delegates are still in the hall, stiff from the coaches, arguing in low voices about where the hearing should sit. Somebody will have to decide what to do with her. Before that, somebody has to decide what the Mother Bell is for.

decisions.label: Leave the Mother Bell for many voices: any town may ask, all may answer

text.narrate: You have the founders' line cut fresh into the rim, where the soot was: Many voices to answer. Under it, the miners add something of their own: ask first.

text.text: That will do. That will do very well.

decisions.label: Take the rope down: nobody rings the Mother Bell again

text.narrate: You and Orin cut the bell-rope down and coil it, and Wren locks it in the forge-signal house, and gives you the only key.

text.text: Nine hundred years they left it hanging. Maybe that was the mistake.
Maybe. Or maybe they were waiting for someone to ask the bells.

oath.name: The Second Oath
oath.region: The council in the casting hall at Cinder Fold
oath.threat: Elske Marrow answers to the council for ringing the Mother Bell alone. She has one more thing to say before they decide, and it is about you. Then she has one more thing to ask, and the Mother Bell is listening.
oath.brief: The council sits at Cinder Fold to decide what to do with Elske Marrow. She has asked to speak first. Answer her, and decide who your oath answers to.

opening.narrate: The council sits in the casting hall, under the Mother Bell, on the floor, because there are still no chairs. All five delegates, and Brannagh's goat, and, at Aveline's insistence, a ward: the little bell that carries Aster Vey's voice, set on a stool at the end of the circle.
The council sits in the casting hall, under the Mother Bell, on the floor, because there are still no chairs. All five delegates, and Brannagh's goat.
Elske Marrow stands in the middle of the circle to answer for what she did. She does not ask for mercy. She asks to speak first, and nobody can think of a reason why not.

opening.text: I rang the Mother Bell alone. I did what I said nobody should ever have to do, and I'd like that written down. But I'd like this written down too.

opening.narrate: She turns, and looks at you.

opening.text: Everyone in this room has watched the same thing for a year. At every town, at every bridge and gate and churchyard, someone decided what happened next. Not a council. Not a vote. You.
At Highpass you put your own fee on the table for Fenmere before the council had agreed to anything, and the council followed you because it was embarrassed.
At Highpass you took Merrowgate's loan for the whole council, because someone had to.
At Fenmere you promised three hundred people a village that no council had agreed to give them.
At Kell's Bridge you decided where forty soldiers would serve.
In Merrowgate you gave away a harbour.
In Merrowgate you named Haverick to a whole hall without a hearing.
You kept the lamp receipts from me, for a vote. I don't blame you. I'd have done the same.
And at Briarwatch, an old woman looked at you before she voted, and you told her which way, and everybody saw it.
To be fair to you: at the bell, when you could have stopped me by hand, you waited for the council to recall me instead. It cost Fenmere its song for a day. I noticed.

I'm not saying you were wrong. I'm saying you are a Warden of the Chorus already. Nobody voted for you. Nobody can recall you. So before you all decide what to do with me, I'd like to know who the hero answers to.

opening.narrate: The casting hall is very quiet.

opening.text: She's not wrong. I hate it, but she's not wrong.

talks.label: Ask your companions what they think, before you answer

lines.text: She's right about the facts. Wrong about what they mean. You decided things. You also came back and told people what you'd decided, every time, and let them shout at you. That's not a Warden. That's a sergeant.
She's asking because she wants to know if there's a way to hold power that she could have lived with. Answer her honestly. It's the kindest thing you can do.
I think you should answer to us. But I would think that.

talks.label: Look in on Pell Haverick in the miners' lock-up

lines.narrate: The miners have put Pell Haverick in their lock-up by the gate, a stone room meant for drunks on pay night. He has been given a chair, a blanket and one lamp, the first lamp in years that he does not own, and he has turned it down very low.
Iona sits outside the grille with a writing desk across her knees, reading to him from a list. She does not stop when you come in.

lines.text: Item: half a pane of ward-glass short on every lamp in the Sallows, sold at the full price. Item: one quartermaster, taken on her way to breakfast. Item: twelve carters, paid to shout. Item: bravos, sent up a mountain, thirty-eight. Your office says forty. I counted.
You make it all sound so deliberate.
It was deliberate. You signed it. You sign everything. It's the one thing I admire about you.

lines.narrate: Haverick turns to you, delighted, exactly as he was in the room with forty lamps.
Haverick turns to you, delighted, as if you had come to buy something.

lines.text: The hero! You'll understand, I think. I never made anybody buy anything. The Sallows wanted lamps it could afford, and I sold it lamps it could afford. The council wanted time to argue, and I sold it time. A bell that answers to one person is a thing people want. Somebody was always going to sell it.
You told the whole auction hall about me, you know, and I wasn't even there to object. I took that very personally. Put it on your list, Quartermaster.
It's on the list. Under 'complaints, the prisoner's'.
And Elske replaced every lamp in the Sallows out of her own salary, and never said one word to me about it. That's when I knew. People who stop arguing with you have stopped needing you.
Those receipts of the lamp-man's. I'd have bought them back from you at a very fair price. Nobody asked me.
Somebody's always going to sell it. That's not a defence. That's a description of you.

lines.narrate: You tell him that somebody always being ready to sell a thing is not a defence. It is a description of him.
Iona writes that down. Haverick smiles, without any malice at all, the way he has smiled at everyone. Then he asks her, politely, whether there is a total.
There is. She turns the desk round so he can read it. For the first time anyone in the lock-up can remember, Pell Haverick has nothing to say.

talks.label: Ask Aster Vey what the wards think

lines.text: The wards think that nobody has ever asked us who we answer to. We answered to whoever held the rope.
I was a keeper, before I was a bell. I answered to the village. Then to Sable. Then, for a while, to nobody, in the dark, under the roots. That was the worst one.

oath.clue: Elske is not asking to be pardoned. She is asking whether power can be held in a way that answers to someone, and she is asking you because you have held it all year without anyone voting for it. The council will decide her fate; your answer will decide how it hears the question.

investigate.label: Think back over the year before you answer

success.narrate: You think it through, the whole year. The chairs, the churchyard, the bridge, the auction, the long room, the burned hall, the lid, the square, the rope. Elske has the list right. She has missed one thing off it: every time, afterwards, you came back and told them.

investigate.failure: The year will not come together in your head. Too much happened. But you know what you would say to the people in it, if they asked, and that will have to do.

route.label: Stand up in the circle and answer her
route.success: You stand up. The council looks at you, and for once, nobody interrupts.
route.failure: You stand up and find you have less to say than you thought. The council waits anyway. They have learned that this year, at least.

direct.label: Answer her plainly, without a speech
direct.text: You don't make a speech. You walk into the middle of the circle and say what you think, in the fewest words you can.

approach.narrate: The circle on the casting-hall floor is wide enough that you have to walk across the middle of it to answer. Elske steps back to give you room. Somebody has found a chair for her, at last, and she does not sit in it.

crisis.narrate: You answer her. It does not take long. And when you have finished, the council has to decide what to do with Elske Marrow, who rang the Mother Bell alone and then let go of the rope.

crisis.text: She was never Warden. We said no. The charter gives nobody the power she used, so it says nothing about what to do with someone who used it anyway. We didn't think we'd need that page.

She was the lawful Warden. She did exactly what the charter let her do, and it silenced every ward in the land. The charter says how to recall a Warden. It doesn't say what to do with one who used the power exactly as written. We didn't think we'd need that page.

We recalled her, lawfully, two-thirds and the paperwork. She let go of the rope when the vote was read. The charter doesn't say what happens to a Warden after that. We didn't think we'd need that page.
We never think we'll need that page.

crisis.narrate: But Elske is not finished. The Gloam is quiet everywhere for the first time in years, and she has seen what one voice does and what many voices do, and she is not sure, standing in the circle, that she can live in the world where the second one is the answer.

crisis.text: I'll go. Wherever you send me. But first I'm going to ask the council to put the Mother Bell under one voice again. Not mine; I've had my turn. Somebody's. Not because I want it. Because one day it will be Hollin's Reach again, and the council will be arguing, and someone has to be able to ring it. I'm asking now, in front of all of you, in daylight. I took, once. I won't again. I'd rather ask.

crisis.narrate: Some of the delegates are nodding. Sorrel is. Iona has her pen out. The miners at the back of the hall are not. And over everyone's heads the Mother Bell has begun, very faintly, to hum: the note from midwinter, the one that silenced every other ward. Nobody has touched the bell-rope. The bell heard her, and it remembers being asked for one voice. Somebody, in the end, has to answer her before the room does: with words, or by getting to the bell first.

Some of the delegates are nodding. Sorrel is. Iona has her pen out. The miners at the back of the hall are not. The bell-rope is coiled in the forge-signal house, behind a lock, and the only key is in your pocket. It does not matter. Over everyone's heads the Mother Bell has begun, very faintly, to hum, with no rope on it at all: the note from midwinter, the one that silenced every other ward. The bell heard her, and it remembers being asked for one voice. Somebody, in the end, has to answer her before the room does: with words, or by getting up the ladder to the great beam and putting a hand on the bronze.

peaceful.label: Persuade Elske to let the council carry it, and to sit with them

success.narrate: You tell Elske the one thing nobody has said to her in eleven years. That the room in Hollin's Reach was not her fault. That seven people had the numbers wrong, not one. That the answer to a slow council is not a fast person but a council that has learned to look at the window. And that you would like her in this one, looking at it with them.
Elske looks up at the humming bell for a long time.
Elske looks up at the great beam for a long time, where the hum is coming from, with no rope on it at all.
Then she says, very clearly, 'I withdraw it,' and the hum dies away to nothing, and she sits down in the chair somebody found for her, in the circle, between Brannagh and the goat.

success.text: It will be slow.
It will. Get used to it. I had to.

failure.text: You can't promise it won't happen again. Nobody can. Then I'll ask the room. Hands, please. One voice for the Mother Bell.

failure.narrate: Sorrel's hand goes up. Then, slowly, Iona's. With every hand the hum above you grows, until the bronze is ringing on its own, one note, louder and louder. Elske hears it and goes white. 'That isn't me,' she says. 'I'm not touching it.' It does not matter. The bell is answering the room. You have to quiet it before the vote is counted.

Sorrel's hand goes up. Then, slowly, Iona's. With every hand the hum above you grows, until the bronze is ringing on its own, one note, louder and louder, with no rope and nobody near it. Elske hears it and goes white. 'That isn't me,' she says. 'I'm not touching it.' It does not matter. The bell is answering the room. You have to get up the ladder and quiet it before the vote is counted.

objective.name: Quiet the Mother Bell before the room rings it
objective.label: Quiet the bell's single note before the room agrees
objective.description: Three successful actions reach the Mother Bell and quiet its single note while the council finds its other voices.
objective.failText: Before you reach it, the Mother Bell sounds one stroke under one voice: the room's, this time, not anybody's hand. Every ward in the land goes quiet for the length of it. It is only a moment. Nobody who heard it will forget it. Sorrel and Iona put their hands down, and Elske, white to the lips, withdraws the proposal herself.
objective.successText: Your hand is on the bronze. Below you, Elske says, very clearly, 'I withdraw it,' and the note dies under your palm.

after.narrate: In the end, the council decides. Slowly. With a great deal of argument, and three adjournments, and one long silence while Iona finds the right page.
Aveline has her pen ready. Before the council rises, somebody is going to want your answer to Elske's question written down. She has, for once, only one bag.

decisions.label: Ask the council to give Elske a seat, without the Warden's power

text.narrate: The council gives Elske Marrow a seat, as Merrowgate's delegate, and nothing else. She takes it. At the next session she redraws the seating chart in five minutes, and nobody minds.

decisions.label: Ask the council to judge Elske for ringing the bell alone

text.narrate: The council judges Elske Marrow for ringing the Mother Bell alone. It takes a week, and it is fair, and it is slow. She is sentenced to exile from the council for five years, and to keep the Sallows hospice open for every one of them. She says it is the kindest thing anyone has done for her since Hollin's Reach.

decisions.label: Ask the council to let Elske go home to Merrowgate, and nothing more

text.narrate: The council lets Elske Marrow go home. No seat, no sentence. She walks down the mountain alone, and at the bottom, Anwen Holt is waiting for her with a cart, a blanket and a pack of cards.

b3-letter.name: The Letter from Vell
b3-letter.region: Briarwatch, in the first week of spring
b3-letter.threat: Frost has ridden into Briarwatch on a Commandery courier's cart, folded into the canvas. At dusk it will get loose in the lanes. Bring light.
b3-letter.brief: A Commandery courier reaches Briarwatch half dead, with a letter from High Warden Corvane for the one who broke the Single Voice. Hear what it says, and find out what came up the road with her.

opening.narrate: Spring comes to Briarwatch the way it always does, late and all at once. The mud on the Briarwood road is ankle-deep, the forge door stands open for the first time since autumn, and every hour the bell in the tower rings twice: once from Tovin, and once, a breath behind him, from Pim.
Pim is fifteen now. He rings exactly on the hour. Tovin has stopped telling him to breathe, because he does.

At the fourth hour of the afternoon a cart comes up out of the Briarwood. The horse is walking because it can no longer trot. The canvas over the cart is white: not snow-white, but frost-white, in a week without a frost, and the white has a grain to it, like the inside of a shell.

The woman on the box wears a Commandery greatcoat with the iron badge cut off it. There is a bandage round one hand, and a satchel strapped to her chest under the coat, the way people carry the one thing they will not lose.

opening.text: That horse wants water and that woman wants a fire. Somebody take the horse.
I have him.

opening.narrate: Orin takes the bridle. The horse leans its whole weight on him and he lets it.
You take the bridle yourself. The horse leans its whole weight on you, and you let it.

opening.text: Sergeant Ama Roke. Courier, Vell to the free wards. I have a letter for the one who broke the Single Voice.
They said you'd be in the village with the bell. They said you'd look tired. You do.
She is frozen through, and not from the road. Sit her by the forge. Now, please.

opening.narrate: Roke will not give up the satchel until she has looked at your face for a long moment. Then she hands it over as if it weighs more than it does, sits down on the mounting block by the forge door, and does not get up again for some time.
Inside the satchel is one letter, sealed in grey wax with the Commandery's iron mark.

Aveline reads it at the long table in the reeve's hall, where the council's business in Briarwatch is done. You swore your oath to the council, she says, so a letter to you is council business. She reads it standing, with her spectacles on and her coat still buttoned.

Aveline reads it in the square, from the step of the well. You swore your oath to Briarwatch, and Briarwatch holds you to it: what comes to you comes to all of them. Half the village is there before she has it unfolded. Tovin stands at the back with Pim, who has brought a lantern although it is not yet dark.

Orin reads it by the fire in the forge. You swore your oath to the people you walk with, and he says that means they hear your letters. He reads slowly, giving every word the same weight, the way he reads orders.
You read it aloud by the fire in the forge. You swore your oath to the people you walk with, and they are owed your letters.

You read it alone, on the bench outside the forge. You swore your oath to no one but what is right as best you can see it, and a letter addressed to you is yours to read first. Who else hears it is yours to decide.

Aveline reads it at the long table in the reeve's hall, with her spectacles on and her coat still buttoned. A letter from the Commandery to anyone in Briarwatch is Briarwatch's business, she says, and she is not going to argue about it.
"To the one who broke the Single Voice, at Briarwatch or wherever this finds you. From Corvane, High Warden, at Vell."
"I will not apologise for the beacon. You would not believe me, and I would not mean it. I will tell you instead what it cost, since nobody else will."

"When the Single Voice went quiet, every echo-stone in the Commandery went quiet with it. They had no other master. We melted down every ward this province had to make them, a generation ago, because one voice was safer than a hundred. I agreed with that. I still think it was nearly right."

"These are the towns the Gloam has taken this winter. Harl. Upper Morrow. Cask. Lindmoor. Greyhythe. The three Teller villages. Brack Mill. Osgood's Cross. Wennet. Saltwick is not taken. Saltwick is on its roofs."
"I write their names because nobody in the free wards has heard them, and somebody should."

"I have found a way to give Vell its wards back. It is quick, and it is willing, and it came to me in your Warden Sable's hand. I would rather you came and saw it than heard about it from someone who has not. Come and see the nurseries. They are under the casting yard, where it is warmest. There are eleven hundred children in them. Count them, if you like. I have."
"Corvane."

opening.text: I cannot hear a letter breathe. I wish I could.
Sable's hand. He said Sable's hand. Sable's in a cell. What's Sable doing writing to—
Nurseries.

opening.narrate: By the forge fire Roke has her bandaged hand round a cup and is not drinking from it.

opening.text: He wrote it four times. I watched him. The first three were longer.

opening.narrate: Up in the tower, the bell rings a quarter of an hour early, once, softly. Tovin looks up. Pim looks at Tovin. In all the years since the bell came back, it has never rung by itself.

talks.label: Climb the bell tower and hear what Aster Vey wants

lines.narrate: The tower stair is narrow and smells of rope. At the top the bell hangs still, and when you put your hand on the bronze it is warm, the way a wall is warm with a fire behind it.

lines.text: He means my rite. Sable's. The one he used on me.

The old keepers had a rite of their own. When a keeper died, if she chose, her spirit could stay in her bell and go on keeping the place. Chose. That was the whole of it. Sable changed the words so that nobody had to choose. You broke his rite before it finished me, and it still took me years to find my own name again.
While he worked, he talked. He told me once that the change had a second use. He was pleased with it. I didn't understand what he meant. I think I do now.
You think Corvane has found the second use.
I think a man who writes about nurseries has found something quick. Take me to Sable before you answer him. I want to hear him say it, and I want you there when he does.
Can you travel?
Tovin has a hand-bell cast from the same pour as this one. I can sit in it for a while. It is like sleeping in someone else's coat.
Does it hurt?

lines.narrate: The bell is quiet for long enough that you wonder if she has gone.

lines.text: Nobody has asked me that before. A little. Ask me again on the road.

talks.label: Find Pim and Tovin on the tower steps

lines.narrate: Tovin and Pim are sitting on the bottom step of the tower with the hand-bell between them, polishing it, although it does not need polishing.

lines.text: Tovin. If a person was in a bell. Would they know what time it was?

lines.narrate: Tovin's cloth stops moving.

lines.text: I only mean, do they hear the hours, or is it all one long hour, or do they sleep in between? Because if they slept, you'd want to ring gently, and if they didn't, you'd want—
Pim. I'm frightened.

I've been frightened since that cart came up the road. I'm telling you because you asked a real question and you ought to get a real answer, and that is the answer. I don't know what it's like in there. I know what it did to her.
I'm sorry. I didn't mean to—
Don't be. Ring the half-hour with me. It helps.
It isn't the half-hour for four minutes.
Then wait four minutes with me.

lines.narrate: They wait. When the half-hour comes they climb the stair together, and the bell rings twice, a breath apart, the way it always does.

talks.label: Sit with Sergeant Roke by the forge fire

lines.narrate: Roke has thawed enough to take her boots off. Her toes are white at the ends. Maren has seen them and has said nothing yet, which Roke has noticed.
Roke has thawed enough to take her boots off. Her toes are white at the ends, and she keeps them close to the fire.

lines.text: Three towns between Vell and the pass are still standing, if you want to call it standing. They live on the roofs. Planks laid between the chimneys, ropes for rails. The lamplighters keep lamps lit all night along the roof-ridges, to hold the mist down in the streets.
I slept on their roofs, all three. Kettle Cross. Dunmow. Saltwick.

lines.narrate: Orin has been mending a strap on his shield. At the third name his hands stop, and stay stopped.

lines.text: Orin?
Nothing. Go on.
Saltwick's lamplighters gave me oil for the cart lamps. They haven't enough for themselves. Their head, a woman called Mags, said take it, and tell them we're up here. So.
They're up there.
Why'd you cut the badge off your coat?
Roof folk don't love the iron badge. You don't get a plank put out for you wearing it. I can sew it back on in Vell, if I get back to Vell.

talks.label: Let Dera look at your gear while there is still light

lines.narrate: Dera has your gear on the bench before you have finished asking. She turns your blade over, sniffs at the edge as if it might be off, and puts it down.

lines.text: That's a week's work, that. I'll take news for it. From Vell. Proper news, mind, not what the whole square heard.

lines.narrate: You tell her the courier's name.

lines.text: That's not news. That's a name. A name's worth a rivet. What's the weather like in Vell?

lines.narrate: You don't know the weather in Vell.

lines.text: What do they eat? Do they have smiths? Good ones? What do they charge? You've had that woman by my fire for an hour and you don't know what a Vell smith charges?
She knows the towns that've gone.
That's the whole square's news. I want something for me.
And don't tell me about the towns that've gone. That's the whole square's news. I want something for me.

lines.narrate: So you tell her about the nurseries: eleven hundred children, under the casting yard, where it is warmest. Dera listens with the blade across her knees.

lines.text: That's too much. That isn't payment, that's... you've overpaid.

lines.narrate: She finishes the work anyway, and when she hands it back she has also sharpened your belt knife, which you did not ask for, and she does not mention it.

b3-letter.clue: The white on Roke's cart is not frost. It is Gloam, folded into the canvas the way damp folds into a tent, and it rode up the Briarwood road with her. At dusk it will look for somewhere warm. Briarwatch's old bell-books say that carried cold was rung back together twice before, both times by two bells ringing at once.

investigate.label: Look at the frost on Roke's cart before the light goes

success.narrate: Up close, the white on the canvas lies in folds, and the folds have moved since noon. Under the cart, the mud has gone grey and hard in the shape of the wheels.

Tovin brings down the tower's bell-books, the old ones, and you go through them together on Dera's bench. Two hundred years of hours, rung and written down. Twice in all that time there is a word in the margin: carried cold. Once a peddler's pack, once a wool-cart from the north. Both times it got loose at dusk. Both times the keeper and a second bell rang it back together into one place, and it was burned.

success.text: Two bells. We have two bells. We have this one, and the hand-bell, and her.

failure.narrate: Up close, the white on the canvas lies in folds, and the folds have moved since noon. Under the cart the mud has gone grey and hard in the shape of the wheels. Whatever it is, it is not staying where it is.
Tovin goes up to look for the old bell-books, and is still looking when the light starts to go.

route.label: Go door to door and get people in and their hearths built up before dusk

success.narrate: You go down every lane in Briarwatch before the light goes. Doors shut, shutters up, hearths built high. Old Mother Tanner wants to know who you think you are. Then she builds up her fire.

success.text: And the forge stays lit. All night. I'll sit up.

failure.narrate: Half of Briarwatch listens. The other half wants to know why, and you don't have a good answer that doesn't sound mad. When the light goes there are still doors open on the Ashford road, and a child chasing a cat down the lane by the mill.

direct.label: Stay in the forge yard and watch the cart
direct.text: You stay in the forge yard with the cart, and let the village find out what is happening the way villages do, by shouting it from door to door.

approach.narrate: The light goes at the sixth hour. Roke's cart stands in the forge yard where Dera put it, and in the last of the light the white on the canvas moves: one fold, then another, like something turning over in its sleep.

approach.text: It did that in Saltwick. On the roofs. I thought I was tired.
Get the lanes clear first. Then the cart.

crisis.narrate: At dusk the canvas lets go of it all at once. The white comes off the cart like breath off a horse, and goes, low and quick, into the lanes.

Where it passes, the warmth goes out of things. A candle in the Tanners' window goes grey and stands there lit and cold. The kitchen fire at the mill sinks to embers in a breath. A dog in the lane by the well lies down and will not get up. Shapes walk in the white: a cart, a horse, a woman with a sack, all of frost, all walking toward the warmest houses in the village.

crisis.text: The bell-books say two bells. Ours and a second, rung together, to call it back into one place. I can ring the tower. I can't ring both.
Tovin. Ring with me. I don't know why. I know it wants two.
Give the hand-bell to someone with steady hands. I'll be the other bell.

crisis.narrate: Pim holds out his hands. They are shaking. Tovin looks at them, and then puts the hand-bell in them anyway.

crisis.text: I'll keep the lane by the tower clear. Biscuit, with me.
Nothing gets up that stair.

peaceful.label: Ring the cold back together with Tovin and Aster Vey

success.narrate: You stand at the foot of the tower and give them the beat, the way the old bell-books mark it: tower, hand-bell, tower, hand-bell, and a breath between.
You stand at the foot of the tower and give them the beat, because somebody has to: tower, hand-bell, tower, hand-bell, and a breath between. You find it by ear, and they follow you.
Tovin rings the tower. Pim rings the hand-bell a breath behind him, the way he has rung every hour this spring, and inside the hand-bell Aster Vey rings with him. The two notes meet over the square.

In the lanes, the white stops. Then it turns, slowly, like a flock turning, and comes back. It comes up the lanes and across the square and into the forge yard, and folds itself back down on the empty cart, and lies there.

success.text: Right. Out of the way.

success.narrate: Dera and Roke drag the canvas off the cart with forge tongs and feed it into the forge, a yard at a time. It does not burn like canvas. It burns like ice on a griddle, hissing, and then it is gone.

failure.narrate: The two notes don't find each other. The tower rings, and the hand-bell rings, and they ring past each other like two people shouting from opposite ends of a field.
The frost-shapes turn toward the sound, and toward the warmest place in the village, which is the forge, and the tower beside it. You will have to hold the lanes while Tovin and Pim find the beat.

objective.name: Ring the carried cold back into the forge yard
objective.label: Hold the lanes while the two bells ring
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the frost-shapes off the tower stair while Tovin, Pim and Aster Vey ring the cold back into one place.
objective.failText: The cold reaches the mill and three houses on the Ashford road before the bells call it back. The families get out. By morning their hearths will light again, but one old man has lost the name of the street he was born on, and does not get it back.
objective.successText: The two bells find each other. The white turns in the lanes and comes back to the cart, and Dera feeds the canvas into the forge.

after.narrate: By midnight the canvas is ash and the lanes smell of wet stone and smoke. The candle in the Tanners' window has gone out at last, as an ordinary candle does. The dog by the well has got up and gone home.
Tovin sits on the tower step with his hands shaking. Pim sits beside him with the hand-bell in his lap and says nothing at all for nearly ten minutes.

There are frost-burns on your hands and on everyone who held the lanes. Up in the tower, Tovin and Pim finished the ringing while you fought, and the last of the white came back to the cart and burned. Tovin sits on the tower step with his hands shaking. Pim sits beside him with the hand-bell in his lap.

There are frost-burns on your hands and on everyone who held the lanes. Up in the tower, Tovin and Pim finished the ringing while you fought, and the last of the white came back to the cart and burned. Tovin sits on the tower step with his hands shaking. Pim sits beside him with the hand-bell in his lap.

after.text: She was in here. The whole time. I could feel her ringing.
You kept the beat, Pim. Nobody ever kept a beat for me before.

after.narrate: Roke is asleep by the forge with the empty satchel under her head. Before she went to sleep she said that she will carry an answer back over the pass, if there is one, as soon as her toes are hers again.

after.text: A week. Not before.

after.narrate: The letter is on the table where it was left. Corvane's hand is very neat. The list of towns takes up most of the page.

after.text: He wants an answer. So does the bell.

decisions.label: Write back to Corvane that you are coming
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Corvane will know to expect you, and will meet you himself.

text.narrate: You write it at Dera's bench, short, because nothing longer comes out right: you have read the names; you are coming to see the nurseries; you will decide nothing until you have.
A week later Roke reads it over twice, folds it into the satchel and straps the satchel under her coat.

text.text: He'll meet you at Vell's gate himself. He'll want to. He doesn't get many answers.
Good. Finally. We go.

decisions.label: Take the letter to the council at Highpass before you answer it
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The council will send someone to Vell with you.

text.text: You swore your oath to the council. This is what that looks like. It's slower.

text.narrate: Aveline copies the letter out twice in her small square hand and sends the copies to Highpass by the morning rider. The council answers in four days.
It sends Quartermaster Iona to go with you to Vell: to observe, to record, and where necessary to object. She writes to say that she will meet you at Highpass and is bringing paper.

text.text: Good. Somebody who reads ledgers.

decisions.label: Tell Aster Vey you will hear her out before you answer Corvane
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Corvane waits for an answer; Aster Vey does not.

text.narrate: You climb the tower again after midnight and tell the bell that the letter can wait. You will take her to Sable first, and hear what she has to say, and what he does.

text.text: Thank you.
Nobody has ever waited for me before deciding something about me. Sable didn't. The council asked, and that was kind, but they were asking about the wards. You're asking about me.

text.narrate: Tovin wraps the hand-bell in a scarf for the road. Pim knitted the scarf.

b3-rite.name: Sable's Rite
b3-rite.threat: Lantern Hall agents are in Highpass under other names, with a hired guide who knows the fort. They want something from the prison. Bring a lantern for the cells.
b3-rite.brief: Take Aster Vey to Warden Sable's cell under Highpass, and hear from him what he changed in the keepers' rite, and why Corvane has it.

opening.narrate: Highpass in spring is wind, mud and new timber. The palisade the mist greyed last year has been rebuilt plank by plank, and the new planks are still yellow. Captain Sorrel meets you at the gate.

opening.text: You want Sable. North stair, all the way down. Mind the third step. It's been loose since the Commandery built this place, and I've had other things to mend.

opening.narrate: Quartermaster Iona is waiting at the top of the north stair with a satchel and a folding stool. The council has sent her to Vell with you, and she has spent the two days before you arrived reading the prison's ledgers, for practice.

opening.text: Observe, record, and where necessary object. Those are my instructions. I intend to do all three.

opening.narrate: Tovin's hand-bell rides in your pack, wrapped in a scarf. Aster Vey has been quiet in it since the foothills.

opening.text: I can hear the mountain. It's very loud. I didn't know stone was this loud.

opening.narrate: Sable's cell was a powder store once: dry, windowless, with a door a foot thick. It has become a library. There are books on the bunk and under it, books stacked against every wall to the height of a man, books on the floor with slips of paper in them like tongues. Every scholar in the free wards who wanted his opinion on anything has sent him a book, and he has given his opinion, in the margins.
He is thinner than he was under Briarwatch. His hair has gone white at the front. He is reading by a lamp turned very low, to make the oil last, and he finishes his line before he looks up.

opening.text: The hero. And—

opening.narrate: He stops. He looks at your pack.

opening.text: You've brought her.
I've brought myself. You don't get to say who brought me.
No. Quite right.

opening.narrate: He moves a stack of books off the only chair, carefully, keeping it in order, and offers you the chair. Then he sits down on the edge of the bunk with his hands between his knees and waits, the way he used to wait in the bell-vault for you to understand him.

talks.label: Ask Sable what he changed in the keepers' rite

lines.text: The old rite is a door. The keeper opens it from inside, when she dies, if she wants to. Most didn't. Those who did kept their bells for a hundred years, and their towns were never cold. The old keepers called it staying.
I put a handle on the outside of the door. That's all. The words are nearly the same.
And the second use. Aster Vey said you were pleased with it.

I was. I am, in the way you are pleased with a proof. Once the handle is on the outside, you need not wait for the keeper to die. Cast the bell around a living person, say the words while the bronze is cooling, and the ward is whole by morning. One night. The old way takes a keeper's whole life of ringing, and then her death, and then her choice.
A living person. In the bronze.
A volunteer. It works far better with a volunteer. The unwilling fight it, and a bell that is fighting itself rings badly. I worked that out from Aster Vey.

lines.narrate: The hand-bell in your pack makes no sound at all.

lines.text: Think of it honestly, all of you, before you look at me like that. Fenmere's keeper lost a verse in one night and a village went under the mist. A bell with a person in it does not forget a verse. It does not get old. It does not go to the council and wait three days for an answer. Every town in the Commandery that died this winter would be alive if it had one bell like that, and one person willing. One.
He's—
He's doing it again.
Doing what?
Making sense.

talks.label: Ask Sable why Corvane has a copy of it

lines.text: He asked.

He wrote to me last autumn. Four pages, in a very good hand, by the Lantern Hall's courier, since nobody else carries a prisoner's letters over the pass. He had read what I did under Briarwatch in the council's own report. He asked whether it could be made to work for a city. He asked whether it could be made gentler.
I told him no, it could not be made gentler. He thanked me for my honesty. Then he asked for the words, and I sent them.
You sent a man a way to put people in bells because he said please.
He asked politely. Nobody had asked me anything in a year. Every book in this room came with a question. His was the only one that mattered.
And I sent him the truth because he asked for it. What he does with it is his.
That's what you said about the bell.
Yes. I've had a great deal of time to notice that, Stoneward. It hasn't changed my mind.
For the record: on what date did the letter leave, and was it copied?
The second week of autumn, Quartermaster, and everything that leaves this prison is copied. Ask the ledger room.

talks.label: Let Aster Vey ask Sable her question

lines.narrate: You take the hand-bell out of your pack and unwrap it and set it on the stack of books between you. Sable looks at it the way you would look at a face.

lines.text: I have one question. I've had it a long time.
Did you know my name? When you did it?

lines.narrate: Sable does not answer at once. The lamp hisses.

lines.text: Yes.

Aster Vey. First keeper of Briarwatch. You had a sister in Ashford called Linnet, and you rang the third hour a little flat, and the village liked it that way and never said. It was all in the tower records. I read everything.
Then you knew who you were doing it to.
I knew. I thought it would be easier if I didn't use your name. It was.

lines.narrate: For a long time nobody in the cell says anything. Somewhere above, the watch changes; boots on the stair, a door.

lines.text: Thank you. I wanted to know whether it was carelessness. It wasn't.
That is better, somehow. You can be angry at a person. I spent a long time angry at nothing.
Do you want to go?
Not yet. I want him to look at me a little longer.

lines.narrate: Sable looks at the little bell. He does not look away.

b3-rite.clue: Sable's letters to Corvane went south with Lantern Hall couriers, the only ones who carry a prisoner's mail over the pass. Highpass copies every letter that leaves the prison into its ledger, and the ledger room under the north stair holds a full second copy of the rite. The Lantern Hall's courier knows where it is, because he paid a clerk to tell him.

investigate.label: Go through the prison's letter ledger

success.narrate: The ledger room is a cupboard under the north stair, with one lamp and a clerk called Abernathy who has been copying prisoners' letters for nine years and has never once been asked about them.

The entry is in his hand: "Second week of autumn. One letter, to Vell, eleven pages. Carried by the Lantern Hall's courier, under seal. Copied in full." The copy is bound into the ledger. Eleven pages of Sable's small hand, with the old words and the new words side by side, and a note in the margin: "This is the line that matters."

success.text: There's a second signature beside the courier's. A week later. "Received: a note of the ledger's shelf and number." Abernathy, what is this?

success.narrate: Beside the courier's mark there is a second entry, a week later, in a different ink: "Received: a note of the ledger's shelf and number."

Abernathy goes the colour of the paper. The courier asked for a copy, he says. He said no. The courier paid him two silver to tell him where the ledger was kept instead, and he did not see the harm in it, because it was only a shelf.

success.text: They'll come for it.

failure.narrate: The ledger room is a cupboard under the north stair, with one lamp and a clerk who does not want to be asked anything. You find the entry: one letter, to Vell, eleven pages, carried by the Lantern Hall's courier, copied in full. The copy is bound into the ledger.
There is something else on the page, a second mark beside the courier's, but the clerk closes the ledger before you can read it, and says the ledger room shuts at dark.

route.label: Keep watch on the ledger room from the north stair

success.narrate: You put the lamp out and sit in the dark on the north stair, above the loose third step, where anyone going down to the ledger room has to pass under you. Nessa takes the drain-grate at the bottom, because she says everyone forgets drains.
You put the lamp out and sit in the dark on the north stair, above the loose third step, where anyone going down to the ledger room has to pass under you.

failure.narrate: You sit up on the north stair with a lamp, which is a mistake, and at midnight you move it, which is a worse one. Whoever is coming will know somebody is watching.

approach.narrate: Highpass goes quiet late. The wind drops. Somewhere in the lower camp a child is crying and then is not. Down the north stair, the ledger room's door is shut, and the lamp behind it is out.

approach.text: If they come, they come down that stair.
There are people in the wall. Four. They are walking very softly.

crisis.narrate: They come up through the old powder drain under the ledger room, not down the stair: four of them, in mountain coats, with a dark lantern between them. Three are Lantern Hall men; you can tell from the boots, which are city boots, and from the way they hold their cudgels, which is the way men hold things they are paid to hold.
The fourth is their guide, the one who knew about the drain. She stops dead with one foot on the ledger-room floor when the light falls on her face. It is Lysa.

crisis.text: Oh, no. No. Not you.
They told me it was books. A collector's errand. Get them in under the fort, get them out with a parcel, and nobody hurt. I've been guiding on the pass since the harbour. It pays.

crisis.narrate: The fourth is their guide: a lean mountain man called Corrin Mabry, who has taken travellers over the pass for twenty years and knows every drain in Highpass because he helped dig half of them. He looks at you, and then at the men he brought, and then at the floor.

crisis.text: I was told books. A collector. I've got four children and no work since the beacon went. Books, they said.

crisis.narrate: The man in front has ink on his cuffs and a soft, pleasant voice. He is Factor Wend of the Lantern Hall, and he says so, because he is not ashamed of it.

crisis.text: I'm sorry for the hour. We've come for one book, and we'll pay for it. Every frightened town in the free wards will buy a ward that is whole in a night. Merrowgate will. Ashford will. The Hall would rather sell it fairly than have it sold badly by someone else, and it will be sold. You can't un-write a thing.
Stand aside, and the Hall will remember it. Don't, and the Hall will remember that too.

peaceful.label: Tell the guide what the book is, and turn them

success.narrate: You don't talk to Wend. You talk to Lysa. You tell her what the book is: the rite that was used on the bell under Briarwatch, made quick, to be sold to every frightened town that can pay.

success.text: The bell.
I stood in the hollow with a lantern while he did that to her. I didn't know her name. I know it now. Everybody does.

success.narrate: She steps back into the drain mouth, so the only way out is past her, and folds her arms.

success.text: Factor. The job's off. You can come back out the way we came in, with me, or you can stay here and explain yourselves to Captain Sorrel. I know which I'd pick. I've been on the wrong side of a hero before.

success.narrate: You don't talk to Wend. You talk to Corrin Mabry. You tell him what the book is: a way to put a living person into a bell, to be sold to every frightened town in the free wards.

success.text: A person. In a bell.
My eldest is fifteen. She'd volunteer. She'd be first in the line, she would, if she thought it'd keep the little ones warm.

success.narrate: He steps back into the drain mouth, so the only way out is past him, and puts his lantern down on the floor.

success.text: Job's off, Factor. You can go back out with me, or wait for the captain.

success.narrate: Wend looks at the way out, and at you, and at the ledger. Then he puts his cudgel down on the ledger-room table, very neatly.

success.text: It will be sold. Not tonight. But you know it will.

success.narrate: Sorrel's watch takes the three of them up the north stair. Nobody steps on the third step.

failure.text: I can't. I'm sorry. I've had nothing since the harbour, and they've paid me for the month.
I can't. Four children. I'm sorry.

failure.narrate: Wend sighs, the way a man sighs at a bad price, and his men come forward with their cudgels. You will have to hold the ledger room until the watch comes down the stair.

objective.name: Keep the rite out of the Lantern Hall's hands
objective.label: Hold the ledger room until the watch comes
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the agents away from the ledger until Captain Sorrel's watch comes down the north stair.
objective.failText: One of the agents gets a hand on the ledger and tears a page out before the watch arrives. It is a page of the old rite, the words for staying. Sable writes it out again from memory before morning, without being asked.
objective.successText: The watch comes down the north stair with lanterns, and the Lantern Hall's men put their cudgels down.

after.narrate: Before dawn you are back in Sable's cell, because there is nowhere else in Highpass to put the ledger where everyone can see it. The eleven pages lie on top of the Ashford Chronicles. Sorrel stands in the doorway. She has not slept either.
Lysa waits at the top of the north stair, sitting on her pack. Sorrel has not decided what to do with her, and says so, and Lysa says that is fair.
Lysa is in the guardroom at the top of the north stair with the Lantern Hall's men. She asked to be put in a different room from them, and Sorrel, after some thought, agreed.
Lysa is in the guardroom at the top of the north stair with the Lantern Hall's men. She asked to be put in a different room from them, and Sorrel, after some thought, agreed.

after.text: I want it out of my fort. I don't much care where.
You should know before you decide. Burn it, carry it, give it to your council. I will still have it.

after.narrate: He taps the side of his head, once.

after.text: That isn't a boast. It's simply where it is. Every word, and the old rite beside it, and the line in the margin that matters. Whatever you do with the paper, you are deciding about the paper.
Then decide about the paper. It's the part we can do something about.
For the record, a paper can be recorded, witnessed and kept under seal. A head cannot.
Paper can be read by people who weren't in this room.
Corvane has one already. If he's got Sable's, he hasn't got the old one beside it. This has both.

decisions.label: Burn the copy here, in Sable's lamp
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. One copy fewer in the world. Sable still remembers it.

text.narrate: You feed it to Sable's lamp a page at a time, because the lamp is small. It takes most of an hour. Sable watches every page go and does not ask you to stop.

text.text: The eighth page was the best thing I ever wrote.
It was the worst thing anyone ever did to me.
Yes. Both of those.
Good. Good. Thank you.

decisions.label: Carry the copy to Vell, so Corvane can see the old rite beside his
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You take the rite over the pass yourself.

text.narrate: You wrap the eleven pages in oilcloth and put them at the bottom of your pack, under the hand-bell. Corvane has the new words. He has never seen the old ones beside them: the door opened from inside, and what the old keepers called staying.

text.text: Then he can read the difference with his own eyes. If he's what his letter says he is, that'll matter.
I don't like riding on top of it.

text.narrate: You move the hand-bell to the outside pocket.

text.text: Give him my regards. He was very polite.

decisions.label: Give the copy to the council, sealed, to keep under its law
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The council keeps the rite and answers for it.

text.narrate: Sorrel seals the eleven pages in the council's strongbox with her own seal and a delegate's beside it, and writes in the prison ledger who holds the key, and why.

Iona seals the eleven pages in the council's strongbox with Sorrel's seal and her own beside it, and writes in the prison ledger who holds the key, and why, and how the key may be used, and by whose vote.

text.text: Good. Now somebody answers for it. Not just whoever's holding it.
A council with my rite in a box. I wonder how long it will be before somebody on it opens the box with very good reasons.
Then I'll ask for a seat on whoever decides.
Then it's a good thing the wards have a seat. I'll be in the room when they do.

b3-pass.name: The Pass in Spring
b3-pass.region: The lower gate of Highpass, and the pass road below it
b3-pass.threat: Six hundred refugees from the Commandery are on the pass road, with the Gloam a mile behind them and frost in everything they carry. Bring light.
b3-pass.brief: Six hundred people have walked over the pass from the Commandery with the Gloam behind them. Get them through Highpass's gate without letting the cold in with them.

opening.narrate: They come up the pass road in the morning, from the south, from the Commandery side: a line of people a mile long, walking. Carts where there are carts. Barrows. A man carrying a door on his back with a sick woman lying on it. Six hundred of them, give or take, and behind them, a mile back down the road, the white.
Captain Sorrel watches them come from the lower gate with her arms folded and her face set.

opening.text: Six hundred people. Forty beds. I did the sum twice.

opening.narrate: The council's delegates are at Highpass for the spring sitting, and every one of them has come down to the lower gate. Aveline, with her satchel. Quartermaster Iona, already writing. Brannagh of Fenmere, with the goat on its rope, who looks at the line on the road and then, for a while, at nothing.

Elske Marrow has come down too, as Merrowgate's delegate, in a plain coat, with no clerk. She says nothing at all. She is watching the white on the road behind the line, and her hand is on the gatepost as if she were holding it up.

opening.text: I know what that looks like. That's what we looked like.

opening.narrate: At the head of the line, a thin man in a Commandery clerk's coat is carrying a wooden box in both arms, the way you carry something that is asleep. Behind him a woman with grey in her hair is pushing a barrow with two children in it and a cradle lashed on top.

opening.text: Captain, the sick will need to come in first, whatever else you decide.
I know what the sick need, Sister. I need to know what's in the carts.
What's in the carts? People's things. What else would—

opening.narrate: Nessa stops. On the nearest cart, the blankets are white at the folds.
On the nearest cart, the blankets are white at the folds.

opening.text: Like Roke's cart.

talks.label: Talk with the woman pushing the barrow

lines.narrate: Her name is Hanne Ostrow, and she is from Cask, and then from Lindmoor. She says it like that, as if they were one place with a long name.

lines.text: Cask went first. Before midwinter. The stone on the green just stopped. No sound. We didn't know it had been making a sound until it stopped, and then we couldn't hear anything else.
We walked to Lindmoor. My sister's there. Was there. Lindmoor took us in, every one of us, put us in the tithe barn with straw. Lindmoor's stone stopped in the second week of the new year.
So I've done this before. Twice. That's why I'm at the front. I know how to do it now. You go at the pace of the slowest cart and you don't look back.
Are those your children?
The boy's mine. The girl's my sister's. The cradle's my sister's too. The baby's mine now. I haven't decided what to tell her yet. She's nine months. I've got time.

lines.narrate: She looks up at the gate, and at the soldiers on it, and then at you, for the first time.

lines.text: Are you going to let us in?

talks.label: Ask the clerk what is in his box

lines.text: Clerk-Major Fennick. Census office, Vell. I have papers for all of this. I have papers for everything.

The box is the census of the lost. Every name from every town the Gloam took this winter, entered and checked. Name, age, town, last known address, ward. I walked it over the pass because it was not safe in Vell, and because I thought somebody on this side ought to see it.
May I hold it while you rest? You've been carrying it for nine days.
No.
Thank you. No. I don't put it down. If I put it down I'm afraid somebody will put something on top of it, and then something else on top of that, and then it's a box at the bottom of a pile.

lines.narrate: Iona looks at him for a long moment. Then she puts her own satchel down on the road beside him, on its own, with nothing on top of it.

lines.text: Then we'll go through it standing up. When there's time.
There's never time.
That's what everyone says to me. I've found that there is, if you're rude enough about it.

talks.label: Find Lieutenant Hal and her company on the palisade

lines.narrate: Hal's company serves the council now, and the council has posted them at Highpass for the spring. They are on the palisade in their council coats, watching the line come up the road. Some of them are saying names under their breath.

lines.text: We crewed the echo-stones. You know that. Half my people did two winters on the Commandery side before Central Command pulled us back to the beacons.

Cask. I did the Cask relay. There was a woman sold eggs at the gate and charged soldiers double, and we paid it, because she was right to. Brack Mill. Wennet. Osgood's Cross. We know these towns. We rang the stones that kept them, when Central Command told us to.
And then we broke the voice that told you.
And then you broke it, and you were right to, and the stones stopped, and these people walked. Both of those, Stoneward. I've stopped trying to make it one thing.
Put my people on the gate. They'll know the towns. It'll help, a little, if the first face they see knows the name of where they're from.

b3-pass.clue: Every town in the line had an echo-stone and nothing else: the Commandery melted down its own wards a generation ago to make the stones, and when you broke the Single Voice at the beacon, the stones went dead with it. Your victory cost these people their wards. And the frost in their blankets, sacks and cradles is not weather. It is the Gloam they walked away from, riding with them, as it rode up the Briarwood road on Roke's cart.

investigate.label: Ask the people in the line what wards their towns had

success.narrate: You walk down the line and ask. Cask: an echo-stone on the green. Lindmoor: an echo-stone by the tithe barn. Greyhythe, Wennet, the three Teller villages: a stone, a stone, a stone. You ask about the old wards, the hearth-bells, the songs, and the old people shake their heads. Melted down, their grandparents' time, to make the stones. One voice was safer than a hundred.
Fennick's census has a column for it. Ward. Every line, in his neat hand: echo-stone. Echo-stone. Echo-stone.

success.text: They went dead the night of the beacon. All at once. I wrote down the hour.

success.narrate: He does not say which night of the beacon. He does not need to. He knows who you are.
On the way back up the line, you put your hand on a cradle blanket. It is colder than the morning. The white at the fold moves under your fingers.

failure.narrate: You walk down the line and ask, and nobody much wants to talk to a stranger from the free wards with a sword. You learn that the towns had echo-stones, and that the stones stopped, and that is all anyone will say.
On the way back up the line, you put your hand on a cradle blanket. It is colder than the morning. The white at the fold moves under your fingers.

route.label: Walk the line down the pass road and bring the stragglers up before the Gloam closes

success.narrate: You go down the road against the line and bring the last carts up: an old man who sat down and would not get up, two boys arguing over a goat, a cart with a broken axle that Orin and four strangers carry the last half-mile between them.

You go down the road against the line and bring the last carts up: an old man who sat down and would not get up, two boys arguing over a goat, a cart with a broken axle that you and four strangers carry the last half-mile between you.
The white is a quarter-mile behind the last cart when you reach the gate. It is not hurrying. It doesn't need to.

failure.narrate: You go down the road against the line, and the white comes up faster than you thought. The last carts come up at a run, and the cold catches you on the road: your fingers go grey and slow, and for a moment you cannot remember which way the gate is. Then you can, and you run.

approach.narrate: By noon the whole line is pressed up against the lower gate, six hundred people and their carts in the switchback below the palisade, and the white has stopped a hundred yards down the road, as if it were waiting to be let in with everyone else.

approach.text: I'm not opening that gate until I know what's coming through it.
Captain, there are children on that road.
I know there are children on that road, Reeve. There are children up here too.

crisis.narrate: It starts in the carts. A sack goes white from the bottom up. A blanket stiffens on a barrow. In the cradle lashed to Hanne Ostrow's barrow, the baby's quilt frosts over at the edge, and the baby, who has slept through the whole pass, wakes up and screams.
Hanne has her out of the cradle and under her coat before anyone else has moved.

All down the line people are pulling back from their own things. The frost does not care. It comes up out of the bundles and the sacks in thin white threads, and the threads lean toward the palisade, toward the fort and its fires, the way plants lean toward a window.

crisis.text: There. That's what's in the carts. If they bring it through my gate, it comes up through my fort.
Then they leave the carts outside.
Everything we've got is on those carts. Everything. I walked my sister's cradle over a mountain.
It'll take what's left of her, if you keep it. The warmth first, then the memory.

crisis.narrate: There is one way to bring them in, and it is to ask six hundred people who have lost everything twice to burn the rest, here, at the gate, and walk into a strange fort with nothing.

peaceful.label: Tell them what the beacon cost them, and ask them to burn it all
peaceful.labelNoLead: Ask them to burn everything they carried, and come in with nothing

success.narrate: You climb up on the gate's mounting step, where the whole line can see you, and tell them the first thing first, because it is true: you broke the Single Voice. You did it because it had to be broken, and when you did, every stone in their towns went dead. Nobody told you that would happen. Nobody told them either.

You climb up on the gate's mounting step, where the whole line can see you. You don't know their towns. You don't know what they have walked through. You tell them so, and then you tell them what the white in their blankets is, and what it will do.
Then you ask them to burn it. All of it. Here, now, and come in with what they are wearing.

Nobody moves. Then Hanne Ostrow gives the baby to Maren, goes back to her barrow, unlashes her sister's cradle and carries it to the brazier by the gate. She puts it on the coals. The frost on it hisses and goes up in a thin white smoke.

Nobody moves. Then Hanne Ostrow tucks the baby deeper into her coat, goes back to her barrow, unlashes her sister's cradle and carries it to the brazier by the gate. She puts it on the coals. The frost on it hisses and goes up in a thin white smoke.

success.text: Third time. You get better at it.

success.narrate: After that, it is only a matter of time. Sacks, blankets, barrows, a door with a sick woman's quilt on it; Hal's people pass them up to the braziers hand to hand, saying the names of towns.
After that, it is only a matter of time. Sacks, blankets, barrows, a door with a sick woman's quilt on it, passed up to the braziers hand to hand.
The white on the road below draws back as the frost in the carts burns, a yard at a time, until it is only mist.
Clerk-Major Fennick is the last. He stands at the brazier with the census box in his arms for a long time. Then Iona opens the lid for him, and puts her bare hand inside, on the papers.

success.text: Warm. You never put it down. Nine days. It never had the chance.

success.narrate: Fennick carries the census of the lost through the gate of Highpass, warm, the only thing six hundred people brought over the pass.

failure.text: No. No. You don't get to break our stones and then burn our cradles. Not you.
No. We've given enough. Let us in with what's ours, or don't.

failure.narrate: The line pulls back from the gate and round its carts, and the frost comes up out of them in white threads, then in shapes, rising at the palisade. You will have to hold it while the braziers do their work.

objective.name: Burn the carried cold at the gate
objective.label: Hold the palisade while the carts burn
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the Gloam at the palisade while the carts and bundles are passed up to the braziers and burned.
objective.failText: The cold gets over the palisade at the north corner before the last carts burn. It takes the warmth out of the lower barracks and two store-rooms, and the soldiers who were sleeping there wake not knowing where they are. By evening they know again. The store-rooms stay cold for a week.
objective.successText: The last cart goes up on the braziers, and the white on the road draws back into ordinary mist.

after.narrate: By evening there are six hundred people at the lower gate of Highpass, in what they are wearing, around the braziers. The braziers are full of ash. The white on the pass road has gone back to being mist, and the mist is thinning.

Hanne Ostrow sits with her back to the palisade and the two children and the baby, wrapped in a soldier's cloak. Somebody has given her a bowl of something hot. She has not eaten it. She is holding it for the warmth.

Fennick and Iona sit on two upturned buckets by the gatehouse lamp with the census box between them and Iona's relief ledgers on her knees. For an hour they go through each other's paperwork in silence, line by line: his names, her stores. Neither of them says a word.
Then Iona leans over, takes his pencil out of his hand, crosses out a figure on the fourth page and writes the right one above it.

after.text: ...Thank you.
You carried the seven.

after.narrate: Up at the council's fire, the delegates are already arguing about what happens now. Six hundred people. Forty beds. A spring still cold in the nights.

after.text: Don't look at me like that. Fenmere has a rise with room on it, and people on it who've been where these people are. I'm only saying.
And Highpass has walls. I'm only saying.
They're all looking at you. They usually are.

decisions.label: Let all six hundred in, and ask the council to feed them
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The council feeds six hundred people until they can be moved.

text.text: Forty beds.
Then six hundred people sleep on the floor of a warm fort. It's been done. It's been done to me.

text.narrate: Iona does the sum on the back of Fennick's fourth page. It is a terrible sum. She signs it anyway.

text.text: Ashford will pay its share. I will be sending everyone an invoice. Including, Captain, you.

text.narrate: The six hundred sleep that night on the floors of Highpass: the mess, the chapel, the corridors, the stables, the north stair. Sorrel walks the fort at midnight and steps over them, one by one, and says nothing at all.

text.text: Nobody left outside. Good.

decisions.label: Bring the children and the sick inside, and camp the rest below the walls
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Highpass keeps its stores; most of the six hundred sleep outside.

text.narrate: Sorrel opens the barracks for the children, the sick, and whoever is caring for them. Two hundred and twelve people. The rest make camp in the lower switchback, under the palisade, with the braziers kept lit all night and Hal's company walking the line.

Sorrel opens the barracks for the children, the sick, and whoever is caring for them. Two hundred and twelve people. The rest make camp in the lower switchback, under the palisade, with the braziers kept lit all night and soldiers walking the line.

text.text: It's what the stores will bear. I'm sorry. I am.

text.narrate: Hanne Ostrow takes the two children and the baby inside, and comes back out again an hour later, alone, to sit with the people from Cask by the brazier.

text.text: I've done the inside. I've done the outside. It's better outside if your own people are there.
It's cold tonight.
It's cold every night, Sister.

decisions.label: Send them on to Fenmere's rise, beside Fenmere's own people
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Two days' walk east, to people who have been where they are.

text.text: Two days east. It's not far, for people who've walked a mountain.
We built on the rise, above the old waterline. Sensible. Dull. Right. There's room up there, if they don't mind a flood plot. I've got one. It'll remind them of home.
There's room on the rise. Not much. We'll dig.
And somebody promised my people we'd have the lower village back one day. When we do, there'll be houses down there with nobody in them. That's six hundred somebodies.

text.narrate: Fenmere's families come over the fell to meet the line on the second day: the people who walked out of the lower village before the winter, with their own carts, to carry the children the last miles. Nobody has to explain anything to anybody.

Hanne Ostrow walks beside Brannagh the whole way. The goat walks between them. On the second evening the baby is asleep on Brannagh's shoulder, and Brannagh is holding her as if she has done it all her life.

text.text: Brannagh. You're crying.
I'm seventy. It's the wind.

b3-saltwick.name: The Last Roof
b3-saltwick.region: Saltwick, a salt town on the Iron Road, living on its roofs
b3-saltwick.threat: Saltwick has lived on its rooftops since its echo-stone died. Its lamps keep the mist down in the streets, and the oil for them is running out. The night tides come higher every week.
b3-saltwick.brief: Saltwick lives on its roofs above the Gloam, and its lamp oil is nearly gone. Orin was here eight years ago, the night his company left. See the town through the next tide.

opening.narrate: The Iron Road goes over the pass and down the far side in long grey switchbacks, and every mile of it there is a post, and on every post there is an echo-stone. They are the size of a loaf, black iron, each with a Commandery number stamped on a plate beneath it. Every one of them is dead. You can tell from twenty yards. A live stone hummed; you felt it in your teeth. These are only iron.
Someone has hung a wreath of dried heather on stone forty-one. Someone else has scratched a name into the plate of stone forty-six, too small to read without stopping. Nobody stops.
Quartermaster Iona walks with the party, as the council sent her to, and writes down the number of every stone you pass, and the date, and the words: not working.
Orin walks at the front all the way down. He has not said anything since the top of the pass. Nobody has asked him to.

You come to Saltwick at dusk, and at first you think it is empty. The streets are white to the height of a man: a thick, slow mist lying in them the way water lies in a ditch, with the doorways and the ground-floor windows sunk out of sight under it.

Then you look up. Saltwick lives on its roofs. Planks run from eave to eave across every lane, lashed down with rope, and the whole town is up there: washing on lines between the chimneys, hens in a coop on the chandler's roof, a cookfire on a sheet of iron, a dozen children doing lessons on the slates of the old salt-hall with their slates on their knees. On every corner, on poles twice the height of the houses, there are lamps, and the lamplighters are going round them on the planks with long hooks, one after another, lighting them against the dark. Where the lamplight falls the mist lies flat. Where it doesn't, the mist rises.

A ladder comes down to the road. At the top of it a woman of sixty or so is looking down at you, with a lamp-hook in one hand and a coil of rope over her shoulder. She has a lamplighter's hands, black at the fingertips.
She is not looking at you. She is looking at Orin.
She looks at each of you in turn, slowly, the way a person looks along a line of faces for one in particular. She does not find it.

opening.text: I know you.

opening.narrate: Orin stops at the foot of the ladder.

opening.text: Salt carts. Eight years ago this spring. You were at the back of the column, with the lantern. You had a beard then. It didn't suit you.
Yes.
Mags Peller. I keep the lamps. I kept them then. You won't remember me. I was the one shouting.
I remember.

opening.narrate: For a long moment neither of them says anything. Then Mags turns her lamp-hook round and holds the end of it down to him, the way you would offer it to someone on the ladder who needed a hand up.

opening.text: Mags Peller. I keep the lamps. You're the free wards' lot, from over the pass. Roke said you might come.
Well. Come up, then. You'll want to see it. All of you. Mind the third rung, and don't look at the mist too long. It looks back.
Orin.
I know. Later.

opening.narrate: He takes the end of the hook, and climbs.

talks.label: Sit with Orin on the salt-hall roof, after the lamps are lit

lines.narrate: He is sitting on the ridge of the salt-hall roof with his boots on the slates and his hands hanging between his knees. Below him the mist moves in the lanes like something breathing. He doesn't look round when you sit down.

lines.text: Captain Odell Varn. That was his name. A hired road company, forty of us. The Commandery paid us to bring salt over the pass for one season. Good pay. I'd never had good pay.

We were here three nights, loading. Then there was a tide. Not like this. Bigger. It came up the valley all at once, like a door opening. And the town had nothing. No bell. Commandery melted it down years before, for the stones, and the stones weren't here yet. They had lamps and a lot of shouting.
Varn had us hitched and moving in a quarter of an hour. High road, over the ridge, carts first. I asked him what about the town. He said the contract was the salt.

lines.narrate: He stops. Down in the lane, a lamplighter's hook knocks against a pole, twice, and a lamp flares.

lines.text: I was at the back. With the lantern. That's the job at the back: you hold it up so the carts behind can see the cart in front. So I held it up. And the town could see us go. All the way up the ridge. I could hear them, and I held it up so they could see exactly where we were going without them.
Fourteen. That's how many they lost that night. I found out later. I've always known the number. I never knew a single name.
That's what I meant, all these years, when I said we left civilians behind once. Once. As if it were a thing that happened one time and was finished.
It isn't finished. It's here. She's here. She remembers my beard.

talks.label: Walk the lamp round with Mags Peller

lines.narrate: Mags walks the planks the way other people walk a road: fast, without looking down, talking. She lights each lamp with one turn of the hook, and checks the oil in each with a dip-stick she keeps behind her ear.

lines.text: After that night, Central Command sent a man to say they were sorry, and set us an echo-stone on the green the next spring, so it would never happen again. And it didn't, for seven years. You could feel it at night, humming. My grandson used to put his ear to it.

Then last year it stopped. Middle of supper. Just stopped. And the mist came up the lanes the same week, and we came up onto the roofs, and we've been up here since. Eleven months. We've had two babies born on the roofs. One wedding. The wedding was on the chandler's, which has the best view, and it was a fine wedding.

The lamps hold it in the lanes. The mist doesn't like light, any more than it likes noise. As long as every lamp's lit, it lies down. If one goes out, it comes up that corner, and you go up and light it again, and mind you don't breathe in. That's the whole of the trade. Nineteen lamplighters. I trained every one.

lines.narrate: At the corner of Cooper's Lane she stops, and looks at you, sideways.

lines.text: You want to know what I think of him. Everyone who comes up the ladder with him is going to want to know that. I'll tell you what I'll tell him, when he asks. Which he will. He's got that look.
I don't know yet. That's what I think. I didn't think I'd ever see his face again, and I've been carrying it eight years, and now it's on my roof, and I don't know.

talks.label: Ask the boy mending the plank bridge what he remembers

lines.narrate: Davin Peller is fourteen and has his grandmother's hands, black at the fingertips already. He is relashing the plank across Salt Street, lying on his front to reach the knots, with nothing between him and the mist but six inches of board.

lines.text: That night? I was six. I remember the bell-man's dog. It was yellow. It got up on the well-house roof and wouldn't come down, and everyone said it was the cleverest dog in Saltwick, because it was the only one that went up.
I don't remember the carts. Gran says there were carts. Were you there?
Yes. I was at the back.
Sorry. I don't remember you at all.

lines.narrate: Nobody answers him. Davin shrugs, and goes back to the knot.
Orin nods, and goes and holds the end of the plank steady while the boy finishes the knot.

lines.text: Vell's going to send us oil. If we send them two names. For the wall. I've put mine down on Gran's slate, but she rubbed it off. I put it back. She keeps rubbing it off.
Someone's got to. Hasn't someone got to?
No. No, someone hasn't. That's not how it—

lines.narrate: Davin pulls the knot tight and sits up on the plank, which moves under him, and doesn't seem to notice.
You tell him no. Nobody has got to.

lines.text: Then how is it?

talks.label: Watch Orin and the lamplighters re-rig the Cooper's Lane plank

lines.narrate: The plank across Cooper's Lane has been creaking all evening, and two lamplighters go out to relash it, and Orin goes with them because he cannot watch someone tie a knot and not have a view on it.

lines.text: Lamplighter's hitch. Two turns and a tuck. Holds anything.
It holds if you're pulling it. It walks if you're standing on it. You want a round turn and two half-hitches, and a stopper on the tail.
A stopper. On a plank. He wants a stopper. Mags! He wants a stopper.
Then give him a stopper and see if he falls off.
